title: Epic: GHA OIDC end-to-end signing flow
description:
## Overview

Enable the full flow: GHA ambient OIDC token → Signet authority → bridge cert with capabilities → signed artifacts — with no secrets stored in the repo.

## ADR Convergence

This epic sits at the intersection of four ADRs:
- **004** (Bridge Certs): Capability-bearing X.509 extensions, the cert format
- **007** (Progressive Identity): Level 3 = enterprise OIDC, bridge cert in identity hierarchy
- **008** (Pluggable Signers): `crypto.Signer` interface enables cloud KMS for authority master key
- **011** (Policy Bundles): Controls who gets certs and what capabilities — currently "anyone with valid OIDC token" (§2)

## The Flow

```
GHA Workflow → ambient OIDC JWT (no secrets)
  → POST /exchange-token to Signet Authority
  → Authority validates token (pkg/oidc/)
  → Policy evaluation: allowed repos/workflows/capabilities (ADR-011)
  → Mint bridge cert with capability X.509 extensions (ADR-004)
  → Signed by authority master key (ADR-008 signer backend)
  → Workflow uses bridge cert to sign artifacts
  → Verification by relying party
```

## Sub-beads

1. Bridge cert with capability X.509 extensions (pkg/attest/x509/)
2. Policy evaluation interface for OIDC subjects (pkg/policy/)
3. Complete bridge cert minting in authority /exchange-token
4. CLI: `signet authority exchange-github-token`
5. GHA workflow: OIDC signing e2e test
6. Git signing with external bridge cert (ADR-007 Level 3)

## Notes

- ADR-008's crypto.Signer is already in LocalCA — cloud KMS just works with no code change. Future bead for KMS backend.
- ADR-011 MVP: existing AllowedRepositories/AllowedWorkflows config IS the policy. Full SCIM bundles are a later epic.
- Authority can run ephemerally in GHA workflow for testing (no cloud deployment needed initially).

title: Bridge cert with capability X.509 extensions
description:
## What

Create `IssueBridgeCertificate()` in `pkg/attest/x509/bridge.go` that mints X.509 certificates with capability URIs embedded as extensions per ADR-004.

## Why

The `/exchange-token` endpoint verifies OIDC tokens and maps capabilities but cannot mint bridge certs (authority.go:1097 is TODO). This bead provides the cert-minting primitive.

## Design (from ADR-004)

X.509 extension with signet OID containing:
```asn1
SignetCapabilityAttestation ::= SEQUENCE {
  version      INTEGER DEFAULT 1,
  capabilities SEQUENCE OF UTF8String,
  audience     SEQUENCE OF UTF8String,
  notAfter     GeneralizedTime OPTIONAL,
}
```

Capability URIs follow: `urn:signet:cap:{action}:{resource}[:{constraint}*]`

The bridge cert is an intermediate CA (`IsCA: true, MaxPathLen: 0`) so it can issue ephemeral certs for actual signing — same pattern as ADR-007 Level 1+.

## Implementation

- New function `IssueBridgeCertificate(ephemeralPubKey, capabilities []string, validity time.Duration) (*x509.Certificate, []byte, error)` on `LocalCA`
- Uses `ExtraExtensions` on the X.509 template for capability attestation
- OID: `1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.1.3` (next in existing signet private OID arc)
- Capabilities encoded as ASN.1 SEQUENCE OF UTF8String
- Cert subject: `CN=signet-bridge, O=Signet`
- Returns cert + DER bytes

## Acceptance

- Unit tests for: valid capability encoding, empty caps, round-trip (encode→parse→verify), cert chain validation (bridge signs ephemeral)
- Verify the issued cert's extension can be parsed back to capability URIs

title: Policy evaluation interface for OIDC subjects
description:
## What

Create a policy evaluation interface in `pkg/policy/evaluator.go` that determines whether an OIDC subject is allowed to receive a bridge cert and what capabilities they should get.

## Why

ADR-011 §2: "The authority currently issues certificates to anyone with a valid OIDC token. There is no organizational policy layer." The existing `AllowedRepositories`/`AllowedWorkflows` in `GitHubActionsConfig` is hardcoded config — not a composable interface the authority can call.

## Design

```go
// PolicyEvaluator determines authorization for OIDC subjects.
type PolicyEvaluator interface {
    // Evaluate checks if a subject is allowed and returns granted capabilities.
    Evaluate(ctx context.Context, req *EvaluationRequest) (*EvaluationResult, error)
}

type EvaluationRequest struct {
    Provider   string                 // "github-actions"
    Subject    string                 // OIDC sub claim
    Claims     map[string]interface{} // Provider-specific claims
    RequestedCaps []string            // Capabilities requested (optional)
}

type EvaluationResult struct {
    Allowed      bool
    Capabilities []string  // Granted capability URIs
    Validity     time.Duration // Cert validity override (optional)
    Reason       string    // Denial reason (for logging)
}
```

MVP implementation: `StaticPolicyEvaluator` that wraps the existing `AllowedRepositories`/`AllowedWorkflows`/`MapCapabilities` logic from `pkg/oidc/github.go`. This is a refactor, not new policy logic.

Future: `BundlePolicyEvaluator` that evaluates signed policy bundles per ADR-011.

## Acceptance

- Interface defined with clear contract
- StaticPolicyEvaluator passes tests for: allowed repo, denied repo, allowed workflow, denied workflow, empty allowlists (allow all), capability mapping delegation to provider
- Authority can be configured with a PolicyEvaluator (consumed in bead 3)

Everything else is solid — clean interface, composable, thread-safe (no mutable state), denial paths tested.

title: Complete bridge cert minting in authority /exchange-token
description:
## What

Wire up the TODO at `cmd/signet/authority.go:1097` to actually mint and return a bridge certificate when a CI/CD platform exchanges an OIDC token.

## Why

The `/exchange-token` endpoint currently verifies tokens, maps capabilities, but returns JSON with capabilities and no cert. This is the glue that connects OIDC verification → policy evaluation → bridge cert minting → PEM response.

## Design

In `handleExchangeToken`, after capability mapping (line 1064):

1. Call `PolicyEvaluator.Evaluate()` (from bead 2) to authorize and get final capabilities
2. Call `LocalCA.IssueBridgeCertificate()` (from bead 1) with ephemeral key + capabilities
3. PEM-encode the bridge cert
4. Return in response JSON as `"certificate": "<PEM>"` field

The response changes from:
```json
{"status": "success", "capabilities": [...]}
```
to:
```json
{"status": "success", "capabilities": [...], "certificate": "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----\n..."}
```

## Dependencies

- Bead signet-882eca (bridge cert minting primitive)
- Bead for policy evaluator interface

## Acceptance

- Integration test: mock OIDC token → exchange → receive valid PEM cert
- Cert contains capability extensions that round-trip correctly
- Cert is signed by authority master key
- Cert's ephemeral public key matches the one sent in the request
- Error cases: invalid token, denied by policy, malformed ephemeral key

title: CLI: signet authority exchange-github-token
description:
## What

Create a CLI command that a GHA workflow can call to exchange its ambient OIDC token for a Signet bridge certificate.

## Why

The example workflow in `docs/examples/github-actions-workflow.yml` references `signet authority exchange-github-token` which doesn't exist. CI needs a simple CLI interface, not raw curl.

## Design

New file `cmd/signet/authority_exchange.go` with Cobra command added as child of `authorityCmd` via `init()`:

```
signet authority exchange-github-token \
  --authority-url https://signet-authority.example.com \
  --token "$GITHUB_OIDC_TOKEN" \
  --output ~/.signet/bridge-cert.pem
```

Or with ambient detection (auto-reads `ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL`/`ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN`):

```
signet authority exchange-github-token \
  --authority-url https://signet-authority.example.com \
  --auto \
  --output ~/.signet/bridge-cert.pem
```

Flow:
1. If `--auto`: fetch OIDC token from GHA environment
2. Generate ephemeral Ed25519 keypair locally
3. POST to `{authority-url}/exchange-token` with token + ephemeral pub key
4. Receive bridge cert PEM
5. Save cert + ephemeral private key to output path(s)

## Acceptance

- `--auto` mode reads GHA env vars and requests OIDC token with correct audience
- `--token` mode accepts explicit token string
- Ephemeral key generated securely, saved alongside cert
- Error messages are clear for: authority unreachable, token rejected, invalid response
- Stdout purity: no debug output on stdout (only cert output or file write)

title: Git signing with external bridge cert (ADR-007 Level 3)
description:
## What

Enable signet-git to use an externally-provided bridge cert (from OIDC exchange) in the signing chain, implementing ADR-007 Level 3.

## Why

ADR-007 Level 3: `signet-git init --oidc https://company.okta.com` — bridge cert comes from external OIDC provider. For GHA: the bridge cert from `/exchange-token` should slot into the git signing chain as: authority master key → bridge cert → ephemeral cert → commit signature.

## Design

New `pkg/git/identity.go`:
```go
type Identity struct {
    MasterKey  *keys.Ed25519Signer  // Machine identity (always present)
    MachineID  string
    UserEmail  string               // Optional (Level 1+)
    BridgeCert *x509.Certificate    // Optional (Level 1+)
    BridgeKey  *keys.SecurePrivateKey
}

func (i *Identity) Level() int { ... }
func (i *Identity) HasUserAttribution() bool { ... }
func LoadIdentity(cfg *config.Config) (*Identity, error) { ... }
```

Updated signing flow in `pkg/git/sign.go`:
- If bridge cert present: master → bridge → ephemeral → commit (3-cert chain)
- If not: master → ephemeral → commit (existing 2-cert chain)

CMS signature includes bridge cert in intermediate chain via `cms.SignOptions{IntermediateCerts: [bridgeCert]}`.

## Stretch goal

This is independent of the authority beads — it's about the client-side cert chain. Can be worked in parallel with beads 1-2.

## Acceptance

- Level 0 signing unchanged (backward compatible)
- Level 1+ signing produces CMS with bridge cert in chain
- git log --show-signature works with bridge cert chain
- Integration test in Docker verifies both Level 0 and Level 1+ paths

title: APAS second-implementer demo on DriftlessAF — prove the standard before rewriting it
description:
Build a working APAS attestation emitted by DriftlessAF (chainguard.dev/driftlessaf), as empirical input to the v0.4.0 profile rewrite (signet-ded9d4). Sequenced BEFORE that rewrite, deliberately: built first, the demo tells us which APAS properties are genuinely universal and which only looked universal because signet was the sole implementation.

## Why this is cheap — verified against the source, not assumed

DriftlessAF already ships the entire L2 substrate. reconcilers/ocireconciler/statusmanager/ writes signed OCI attestations via Sigstore keyless: secant.AttestBundle for signing, Fulcio for identity, Rekor (incl. SigningConfigRekorV2) for transparency, sigstore-go/pkg/verify with WithExpectedIdentity for verify-on-read. Direct deps already carry sigstore/cosign/v3, sigstore-go, in-toto/attestation, in-toto-golang.

APAS therefore contributes NO signing, transport, or verification. The seam is a single argument:

    secant.NewStatement(subject, payload, predicateType)

predicateType is currently https://statusmanager.chainguard.dev/{identity} carrying Status[T] (reconciliation status). An APAS predicate is a different type string and a different marshaled body through the same call.

## Predicate body sources (both already exist)

- agents/agenttrace.Trace[T] — ID, OTelTraceID, InputPrompt, ToolCalls[] (ID/Name/Params/Result/Error/Recoverable/Terminal), Turns[] RecordedTurn (per-turn model, token counts, Errors[], Failed), Reasoning[], AgentName, Model, Source, Start/EndTime; plus ExecutionContext (ReconcilerKey, ReconcilerType, CommitSHA, TurnNumber, RequestID).
- agents/checkpoint.Envelope — ReconcilerKey, RunID, Turn, RemainingTurns, Reason, PendingToolCalls[], ConfigDigest. ValidateForResume is fail-closed on schema/provider/model/digest mismatch (ErrConfigDrift). DigestJSON deliberately covers model params, tool definitions, and provider SDK version.

## The two shape conflicts this must surface

1. The unit of work is a reconciler key reconciled to convergence, NOT a dispatch. There is no dispatching agent to name as a distinct entity — the L2 gap.
2. A run suspends and resumes across process boundaries; RunID, not the process, identifies it. APAS's current continuous-execution model cannot describe this. ConfigDigest is already exactly the "what changed under the pause" claim an attestation wants to bind.

## Caveat

DriftlessAF pins sigstore-go back to v1.2.2 via replace because gitsign's validatingRekorClient does not satisfy v1.3.0's sign.RekorClient (sigstore/gitsign#861). A demo built against it inherits that pin.

title: GitHub Release binaries ship unsigned — no cosign anywhere in the repo
description:
Found 2026-08-04 during a cross-repo supply-chain sweep from notme. Verified against this tree.

FINDING: .github/workflows publishes release artifacts via softprops/action-gh-release, and there is NO cosign anywhere in the repo — `grep -rl cosign .github/workflows/ Taskfile.yml` returns zero files. Release binaries are downloadable with nothing attesting where they came from.

WHY THIS ONE IS SHARPER THAN THE CONTAINER CASE: signet is the identity server. Its binaries are what other systems in this ecosystem trust to establish identity — notme's own docs point at signet for the APAS spec and bridge-cert protocol. An unsigned binary from the identity component is the worst artifact in the set to leave unattested, because a consumer has no way to distinguish a real release from one uploaded by anyone who obtained release-write access.

The repo already grants `id-token: write` in 6 places, so the OIDC identity that keyless signing requires is present and in use. The gap is the signing itself, not the plumbing.

WHAT TO DO — binaries, not images, so it is `cosign sign-blob` rather than `cosign sign`:

1. `cosign sign-blob --yes --bundle <artifact>.cosign.bundle <artifact>` for each published binary, and upload the bundle alongside it. The bundle form keeps the signature, cert and Rekor entry in one file the consumer fetches next to the artifact.
2. VERIFY IMMEDIATELY AFTER SIGNING, in the same job, with `cosign verify-blob --bundle` against `https://github.com/${GITHUB_WORKFLOW_REF}` as an EXACT identity, not a regex. A signature nothing checks is indistinguishable from one that silently did not happen — notme shipped three npm releases whose `--provenance` flag was a no-op for exactly that reason (notme-77ead7), and notme's own images were signed-but-never-verified until PR #65.
3. Document the consumer command with the identity pinned to the release WORKFLOW, not just the repo. notme's published command used `^https://github.com/agentic-research/notme/` with no terminator, which matched ANY workflow in the repo — so any workflow holding `id-token: write` could produce a signature that passed it.

Also worth considering here specifically: SLSA provenance via actions/attest-build-provenance, since consumers of an identity binary have more reason than most to want the build inputs attested and not only the output signed.

See notme docs/design/016-signing-surfaces.md and notme PR #65 for the working reference.

NOT proposed as a shared GitHub Action from notme, deliberately: a verify step supplied by another repo means a mistake or compromise there silently neuters the check everywhere it is used, and the check exists to catch precisely that. Independent duplication is correct for verifiers.

comments.text:
PR #144 opened — https://github.com/agentic-research/signet/pull/144

Implemented against the acceptance criteria:

- **Every published artifact gets a cosign bundle.** `release.yml` signs each `signet-*` binary plus `checksums-sha256.txt` with `cosign sign-blob --bundle`. Bundles land in `release-assets/`, which `files: release-assets/*` already globs, so they upload alongside.
- **Verified in the same job.** `cosign verify-blob --bundle` runs per artifact immediately after signing, against `--certificate-identity "https://github.com/${GITHUB_WORKFLOW_REF}"` (exact, not regex) and `--certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`.
- **Release fails if verification fails.** Confirmed by execution, not inspection: tampered blob → cosign exit 1; the `set -euo pipefail` loop aborts on it; the `Create GitHub Release` step never runs.
- **Consumer instructions pin the workflow, not the repo.** New README "From a Release" section — the repo previously documented no release-binary install path at all. Identity is `.../.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/$VERSION`, with an explicit note that loosening to a repo-level regexp lets any workflow holding `id-token: write` satisfy the check.

Two things worth recording beyond the criteria:

1. The `release` job had `permissions: contents: write` only. `id-token: write` had to be added — keyless signing was not previously possible from that job even if someone had tried.
2. First draft's empty-artifact guard was `artifacts=(signet-* checksums-sha256.txt)` checked for length 0. `nullglob` drops an unmatched glob but not a literal, so with zero binaries the array is length 1 — the guard could never fire while reading as a safety net. Same shape as the fixture fixed-point problem in notme's ADR-016 rule 7: a check that passes by construction. Now guards the `signet-*` glob specifically; both branches tested.

cosign pinned to v3.1.1 (the installer's default is v3.0.6) so CI runs the exact version the round-trip was exercised against.

Leaving open until #144 merges.
comments.author: rsry-mcp

comments.text:
Merged as `24e9d1e` (PR #144, squash). All four checks green: Pure Go, PKCS#11+CGO, Security Checks, Performance Benchmarks.

**Verification record.** The signing step only runs on tag pushes, so PR CI does not exercise it. Rather than leave that unproven, the `run:` block was extracted verbatim from the committed workflow and executed locally against fake artifacts, with a shim translating the keyless flags to key-based ones (cosign v3.1.1 — the version now pinned in the workflow):

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| 3 binaries + checksums | 4 bundles written, all `Verified OK`; the `signet-*` glob expands before the loop so bundles are not re-signed |
| Binary substituted after signing | `invalid signature`, exit 1, loop aborts before the remaining artifact — release step unreachable |
| Zero binaries in `release-assets` | guard fires, exit 1 |

One caveat worth recording: the first tamper run "passed" for the wrong reason — `cd` clobbered `$OLDPWD`, so the shim failed on a missing key file rather than a signature mismatch, and still exited 1. Rewritten with absolute key paths plus a clean-run sanity assertion (must exit 0) before the tamper case, so a shim breakage cannot be mistaken for a caught tamper. Same failure class as ADR-016 rule 7 — a check that passes by construction proves nothing.

The next tagged release is the first real end-to-end exercise; if Fulcio/Rekor behave differently than the key-mode shim, the release fails loudly at the verify step rather than publishing unsigned, which is the correct failure direction.

title: "Bridge certificate" names four different things across signet, APAS and notme — and notme is the outlier by one tier
description:
Filed BY notme, FOR signet, because APAS and ADR-004 are signet's and the decision is signet's as much as notme's. It BLOCKS notme's delegation middle tier (notme-600df1 / ADR-019 D4), which should not be built until the name is settled.

signet ADR-004 already flags part of this itself, in a Terminology note: "Bridge certificate is used in two contexts in this codebase." Counting APAS and notme brings it to four.

  1. signet ADR-004 (TARGET DESIGN) — ephemeral, single-use, binds a public identity's verified PROPERTIES to an anonymous session's ephemeral key. A privacy/selective-disclosure mechanism. Position: LEAF.
  2. signet ADR-004 (AS-BUILT) / ADR-006 / integration-seams — MCP client identity cert, email CN, 24h TTL. Position: LEAF.
  3. APAS §3.4 — "The bridge cert IS the dispatch's identity", short-lived, PER-DISPATCH; one Actor produces many dispatches each with its own. Position: LEAF.
  4. notme ADR-008 / ADR-019 — the MACHINE tier, CA=true pathlen=0, minting task certs beneath it. Position: INTERMEDIATE.

THREE OF FOUR PUT THE BRIDGE AT THE LEAF. notme puts it in the middle.

── THE RESOLUTION IS SMALLER THAN THE MESS SUGGESTS ──
ADR-004 also defines a DELEGATE CERTIFICATE: chains to the public root, EKU id-kp-signet-bridge-delegate, and "enables local bridge cert issuance without public root online." That is exactly what notme's proposed middle tier is for — a machine minting locally with no round trip to the authority.

  signet:  public root  →  DELEGATE (intermediate)  →  BRIDGE (leaf, per-session)
  notme:   root         →  BRIDGE   (intermediate)  →  TASK   (leaf, per-task)

STRUCTURALLY IDENTICAL — same depth, same shape, same purpose per tier. The sole disagreement is which tier the word "bridge" names. signet's DELEGATE is notme's BRIDGE; signet's BRIDGE is notme's TASK. The vocabulary is offset by exactly one tier, and APAS sides with ADR-004.

── A CONSTRAINT NOTME MUST HONOUR EITHER WAY ──
ADR-004: "Relying parties MUST accept exactly one intermediate certificate (the delegate) between the public root and the bridge certificate. This prevents downgrade attacks." That is pathlen=1 at the root and matches notme ADR-008's budget — but it means notme's root→bridge→task chain presents one intermediate to a signet relying party ONLY IF notme's bridge occupies the delegate slot. Any further tier breaks signet's verifier. Worth stating explicitly in ADR-004 as a cross-implementation invariant rather than a downgrade-attack aside.

── THE ASK ──
Q1. Which naming wins? notme adopting signet's names is more likely right — two documents already agree, and it keeps notme chains verifiable by signet relying parties unchanged. It is expensive on notme's side (the `bridgeCert` scope, `mintBridgeCertPair`, ADR-008, and the deployed cert profile all carry the current name), but a rename in one repo beats a permanent ambiguity across four documents.
Q2. Does ADR-004's one-intermediate rule bind notme's chain? Reading it as a cross-implementation invariant, notme cannot add a tier without signet's verifier changing.
Q3. "ACTOR" ALSO COLLIDES. APAS's Actor is the agent PERSONA — "a definition, not a running instance". notme ADR-019's `actor` is the key-holder, which is APAS's IDENTITY. Same word, different referent, one stack. notme does not currently model persona at all; if APAS's decomposition is canonical, notme should adopt Owner/Machine/Actor/Identity wholesale rather than parallel vocabulary.

── SEPARATE, SMALLER: ADR-004's implementation note is STALE ──
It describes the deployed certs as carrying "the user's email as CN, Clerk subject ID in an extension … 24-hour TTL" for MCP client authentication. notme has since moved to passkeys with principalId and a 5-minute TTL, and there is no Clerk in the path. The note describes a deployment that no longer exists, and it is the kind of drift that makes a reader trust the rest of the document less.

CROSS-REFS: notme-600df1 (ADR-019, the delegation model and its D4 middle tier), notme-acc822 (chain-narrowing constraints — related, since pathlen is the depth bound), cloister-c10ff2 (a separate cross-repo ask, on the Interlace commitment).

title: design: ADR-012 DPoP-shaped presentation profile is a signet-authored spec + conformance vectors, not notme-only
description:
notme ADR-012 (sender-constrained OIDC) §6 defines a DPoP-SHAPED presentation profile: the challenge-response proof a holder signs to demonstrate possession of the cnf.jwk key (RP-supplied nonce + target URI + method, <=60s, jti single-use, explicitly NOT called DPoP per RFC 9449's access-token scoping). ADR-012 currently scopes it as notme-only.

PLACEMENT REVIEW (this session): that profile will have a TS issuer (notme), TS verifiers (cloister, rig), and potentially Go ones — exactly the multi-language shape that drifted THREE ways for plain DPoP this session (notme gen/ts 603L, cloister vendor 613L, rig 219L missing jti/iat = a live replay hole). The cross-language identity CONTRACT belongs with an authority + pinned vectors, and signet is already that authority (signet-248d17 does canonical kid + vectors). LLO is the crypto-primitive substrate (sign/cas), NOT the auth layer; signet is the Go auth/identity substrate + owns docs/oidc-provider-pattern.md.

SO: the presentation profile should be a SIGNET-authored spec + conformance vectors (same pattern as kid), with notme/cloister/rig conforming — not a notme-only invention. This gives ADR-012 Phase 1 a SECOND signet dependency beyond invariant (v)'s kid.

Cross-link: notme docs/design/012-sender-constrained-oidc.md §6; depends conceptually on signet-248d17 (the authority+vectors pattern this reuses).

title: Dolt runtime state and migration backups were committable
description:
Housekeeping found while starting signet-9b0ecd, 2026-08-04.

`.beads/` runtime artifacts were matched by nothing in .gitignore, so all of them were committable:

  .beads/dolt.bak/        — `rsry bead migrate --commit` renames dolt/ to dolt.bak/ and never deletes it. A binary store (rosary-05fbe0).
  .beads/dolt-server.log  — regenerated on every start
  .beads/dolt-server.pid
  .beads/dolt-server.port

None of these belong in git. The .bak directory is the one that actually matters — it is a whole binary database, so committing it would be both large and confusing to anyone who later wonders which store is authoritative.

Fixed by extending .gitignore. Verified in both directions: all four patterns now match, and `.beads/beads.jsonl` — which MUST stay tracked, since it is the committed export the bead tooling reads — is unaffected.

Same class as a finding in notme the same day: `.gitignore` there had `!worker/**`, a negation broad enough to silently re-include `worker/.dev.vars` (wrangler's standard LOCAL SECRETS file) along with .env, *.pem and *.key across four subtrees. Worth knowing the shape: an ignore file that re-includes subtrees needs its exclusions checked in BOTH directions, because the failure is silent and in the permissive direction. notme now has a test asserting it (worker/src/__tests__/gitignore-secrets.test.ts); signet may want the same if more negations get added here.

title: W4/W6: adopt the mache find-smells gate in signet (commit baseline)
description:
Analysis-substrate decade, W4+W6. signet (Go, key-exchange/identity) currently has no bespoke structural rules — pure adoption: add the mache find-smells GHA (uses: agentic-research/mache/.github/actions/find-smells@<sha>) + a `task smells` local target over signet's Go tree, commit a smell baseline (grandfather current debt). Low-effort adopter — nothing to port or delete, just gain the shared structural gate. Pin mache >= v0.11.0 (the release that ships the ratchet gate).

Depends on mache W6.1 (mache-4dbad9, the reusable GHA) + W5.3.

title: APAS v0.3.0-draft: content origin attestation — the L3→L4 bridge from cloister's ADR-0065
description:
Cloister shipped ADR-0065 (origin sets on receipts) and its implementation answers a question APAS currently leaves open: L3 proves the boundary held, L4 demands attested inputs, and nothing in between says what it means for content to have a KNOWN ORIGIN. Cloister now has that vocabulary in code (src/wire/origin.ts, 326 lines) — OriginEntry(uri, vouchedBy) where vouchedBy is an authority identifier rather than a boolean, unionOrigins as the compose operation, deriveConfidence → origin-attested / origin-asserted / origin-unknown failing closed on the empty set, and mayAttestFully admitting only origin-attested.

APAS needs a draft that adopts this so the standard can WIDEN what content an agent may consume while keeping its safety claims honest — content becomes admissible because it carries origin + confidence, not because it appears on a hardcoded safelist.

Load-bearing points the draft must carry, each learned from the implementation rather than invented:
1. Actor ≠ proposition. Cloister's first cut unioned the submitter into every content origin set, which inverted the incentive: declaring nothing yielded origin-attested while honestly declaring an untrusted source yielded origin-asserted — silence outranked honesty. Who SUBMITTED is a fact about an actor; where content CAME FROM is a fact about a proposition. Mixing them lets an authenticated identity launder into content provenance.
2. vouchedBy is deployment-relative. The ingest point cannot know the evaluator's trust set, so it records WHICH authority vouched, and confidence is derived at evaluation time against that evaluator's trusted set.
3. Origin is accountability, not safety. A vouched host serving attacker-controlled content still yields a vouched origin. The standard must say this out loud or implementers will read origin-attested as 'safe'.
4. Origin sets are disclosure surface. Receipts commit to originsHash, never the set, because a receipt rides a response header and source URIs there would publish an agent's read history — a richer oracle than the peer-existence one already present.
5. Empty vouchedBy is an ordinary, expressible state ('ingested, unvouched'), not an error and not an absence.
6. Bounded, refused-not-truncated: MAX_DECLARED_ORIGINS=64, MAX_ORIGIN_URI_LENGTH=2048, refused rather than truncated because truncation would record a claim narrower than the caller made.

Also resolve the two documented disagreements this touches: cloister-d89c8e (§7.6 assigns L3 to rosary while the isolation substrate is built in cloister+LLO) and §7.5 listing cloister under 'Adjacent Systems (Not APAS Conformance)' — which is now stale in a specific, checkable way.

Deliberately NOT claimed by the draft: this does not make cloister L4-conformant. Per ADR-0065's own scorecard two of five L4 requirements remain partial, and L4's runtime-SBOM requirement is only approximated by ADR-0041 image pins.

comments.text:
APAS v0.3.0-draft is on PR #160 (branch docs/signet-a4200d-apas-v030-origins, 3 commits). Adversarial review found two blockers in my first cut, both real and both fixed — recording them because the first one would have shipped a spec that cannot interoperate with the implementation it claims to adopt:

BLOCKER 1 — vouchedBy cardinality. I wrote "a set of authority identifiers". The implementation has `readonly vouchedBy: string` — a SINGLE identifier, empty string meaning ingested-and-unvouched; set semantics come from multiple (uri, vouchedBy) pairs. My version broke the canonical-ordering rule outright: no comparator is defined over arrays, so two conforming implementations could not agree on encoded bytes, which is the one property originsHash depends on. Verified against src/wire/origin.ts before fixing rather than taking the reviewer's word. Corrected, with the reasoning stated in the spec: two authorities means two entries, which keeps the comparator total over a pair of plain strings.

BLOCKER 2 — the worked example put the full origin array inside a signed DSSE predicate, contradicting the privacy MUST sitting beside it. The rule was underspecified: I had written it as a property of artifact kind when it is a property of WHO CAN READ THE CARRIER. Now: broadcast carriers (a response header, a public attestation feed) MUST carry only originsHash; scoped carriers (a record already restricted to entitled parties) MAY carry the array; default to the digest when unsure. Plus the sentence that closes the trap: signing establishes integrity, never confidentiality.

MAJOR — the widening argument conflated claim-integrity with actual risk. The draft now says plainly that content origin does NOT make a wider corpus safer; it converts an invisible risk into a measured one, and points at §5.1's own row (poisoned input: attributed, not detected) as the residue. This is the paragraph most likely to be quoted out of context, so it now refuses to overclaim in its own text rather than relying on a caveat elsewhere.

MAJOR — §7.6 flattened the mostly-shipped boundary mechanism into the same "Target" label as unstarted work. Boundary and attestation are now separate rows with separate statuses.

Reviewer confirmed sound, checked against source: the confidence-tier definitions, the bounds/refuse-not-truncate rule, the actor-vs-proposition category line, and the §7.5 L3-mechanism claim.

SEPARATE ISSUE, raised by the user and larger than the origin work: the document named one ecosystem's products ~71 times across its NORMATIVE sections while claiming implementation-agnosticism in its abstract. Fixed in commit 0a262a8 — added a Roles table (orchestrator, identity authority, signing primitive, isolation substrate, work-item tracker, context projector, predicate namespace) mapping each role to its reference implementation once, converted normative prose to role nouns, split Normative References into External (all a second implementer strictly needs) and reference-implementation evidence (marked as not required reading), and genericized the worked example. Normative-section product names: ~71 → 13, all of which are now either the Roles table itself or the declared predicate-namespace constant. The one real coupling is stated plainly rather than hidden: the predicate namespace is a single organization's domain, so implementations MUST match those URIs literally and MUST NOT dereference them.
comments.author: rsry-mcp

comments.text:
Full review report arrived after I had already acted on the extracted findings; re-checking it line by line surfaced two items my first fix pass did not actually close, now fixed in 9b84741:

1. BLOCKER 2 was only half-fixed. I rewrote the privacy rule to be carrier-based and annotated the example, but the reviewer's concrete ask was "no digest-only example is shown anywhere" — and that was still true. §3.2 now shows the broadcast-carrier variant of the same predicate, and adds the rule that contentOrigins and originsHash are MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE: an attestation carrying both publishes, on a broadcast carrier, the exact set the digest exists to withhold, so it is malformed rather than merely redundant. That rule did not exist in any earlier revision and is the thing that makes the carrier distinction enforceable rather than advisory.

2. The NIT was a real gap, not cosmetic. "Meaningful at any level from L2 upward" asserted a floor with no reason. The reason turns out to be the argument for why origin is not an L1 feature at all: an unsigned origin record is not evidence — at L1 the same party that chose what to consume also writes the record of what it consumed, and can revise it afterwards. Origin needs L2's tamper-evidence to mean anything to a third party. Now stated.

Everything else in the full report matches what I had already fixed from the extracted findings: vouchedBy cardinality (verified against origin.ts:47 and deriveConfidence's trustedAuthorities.has(o.vouchedBy) before changing anything), the widening argument (now says plainly that widening trades a preventive control for a detective one, rather than claiming honesty covers it), and the §7.6 L3 split into a Partial boundary-mechanism row and a Target attester row.

On the reviewer's MINOR 2: they asked that if APAS wants a stronger absent-vs-empty distinction than the reference implementation provides, it say so as an APAS-only rule rather than "as implemented". The current text concedes exactly that — it names originsDigest's byte-identical treatment as the reason a carrier may lose the distinction, and states that nothing normative depends on it. No further change.

All four JSON examples parse. PR #160 now has 4 commits.

title: Answer decision 0.2: "bridge cert" names four different artifacts — and the rename is cheap, not high-risk
description:
Answering the notme road-map's decision 0.2 ("What is a bridge cert?", owner signet + you, rated "high — a rename after shipping breaks consumers"). Evidence from signet's code, not its prose.

FOUR DISTINCT ARTIFACTS CURRENTLY SHARE THE NAME. They differ in X.509 shape and in lifetime by four orders of magnitude:

1. INTERMEDIATE CA — pkg/attest/x509/bridge.go:58-63: IsCA true, MaxPathLen 0, MaxPathLenZero, KeyUsage DigitalSignature|CertSign. Issues ephemeral end-entity certs, cannot issue further CAs. Documented at docs/setup-github-actions-oidc.md:125 ("IsCA: true (can issue ephemeral end-entity certs)").

2. SINGLE-USE END-ENTITY — docs/design/004-bridge-certs.md:40: "ephemeral, single-use X.509 certificates that bind a public identity's verified properties to an anonymous session's ephemeral key". Single-use and issuing-further-certs are mutually exclusive, so this is not (1). That file already carries an implementation note (:7-9) conceding the deployed certs do not match its own ASN.1 structure.

3. THE /cert/gha PAIR — two end-entity certs, ~5 minute TTL. cmd/sigstore-kms-signet/enroll.go:308-336 validates the signing one strictly as a LEAF: public key must equal the ephemeral signing key, validity window checked, identity URI required in SANs. It is then handed to cosign as --certificate with the CA bundle as --certificate-chain. Nothing anywhere treats it as a CA. "Bridge cert" is also singular where the artifact is a pair.

4. A 365-DAY GIT CERT — cmd/signet-git/bridge.go:28,60: --bridge-validity-days defaults to 365, written to ~/.signet/git/bridge-cert.pem. Same word, a lifetime 100,000x longer than (3).

THE FINDING THAT CHANGES THE RISK RATING: the wire contract does not use the word at all. cmd/sigstore-kms-signet/enroll.go:58-70 shows /cert/gha returns {"certificates":{"mtls":...,"signing":...},"identity":...,"scopes":...,"expires_at":...,"binding":...,"authority":{...}}. The field names are already precise — mtls and signing. The only wire-visible occurrence of the word anywhere is a scope VALUE, "bridgeCert" (enroll_test.go:172).

So a rename does not break the protocol. Blast radius is prose, the gha-identity.yml output names (notme_cert / notme_signing_cert), and one scope string. 0.2 should be re-rated from "high — breaks consumers" to LOW, which matters because it is currently modelled as the long pole gating all of Phase 2.

RECOMMENDED VOCABULARY, chosen so each name states the X.509 shape a verifier must expect:
- "delegated CA" for (1) — it is a CA; calling it a certificate hides that it may issue.
- "enrollment certificate pair", members "mTLS certificate" and "signing certificate", for (3) — matches the wire fields already in use, and enroll.go's own internal naming, which is more honest than the docs.
- "git signing certificate" for (4) — its lifetime alone means it must never be confused with (3).
- Retire (2)'s usage or rewrite 004 to describe whichever of the above it actually meant; its own implementation note says it describes nothing that shipped.

Load-bearing reason to fix rather than tolerate: the CA-vs-leaf distinction changes what a verifier must DO — path length, whether the cert may issue, which EKU applies. A reader who learns "bridge cert" from 004 and then validates a /cert/gha response will build the wrong verifier.

comments.text:
RE-RATED LOW → MEDIUM. notme checked my claim rather than accepting it and found two places I understated the cost. Both corrections are right and both are places I under-checked: I grepped cmd/ and pkg/ for Go wire structs only, and did not look at the DER-encoded scope values or at notme's Cap'n Proto schema.

1. bridgeCert is not merely "one scope string". It is DER-encoded into every issued certificate at OID_SCOPES (notme cert-authority.ts:325). Certificates already issued carry it permanently and cannot be rewritten, so verifiers need a dual-accept window across both names — the same shape as their ACCEPT_LEGACY_DIGEST_BINDING migration. I flagged the scope as wire-visible but then dismissed it as trivial in the same breath, which was the error.

2. BridgeCertResult is a Cap'n Proto struct (notme schema/identity.capnp:62) whose TypeID derives from its NAME — 0x8b5e0c952601cb1f. Renaming changes the TypeID, which is a schema break for typed consumers. I missed this entirely. Mitigated on their side: gen/go has no in-repo consumers (disposition open as notme-ea5c65) and @notme/contract is private.

So: no protocol break, but a signed-value migration plus a schema decision. Medium is the right rating. The load-bearing half of the re-rating survives — this is not a risky rename gating all of Phase 2.

ACTION ITEM BACK TO SIGNET, and it is worse than the misnomer notme flagged. They noted that adopting "Issuing CA" makes docs/design/004-bridge-certs.md:118's EKU name id-kp-signet-bridge-delegate a misnomer (OID opaque, so nothing breaks). True — but reading that section surfaces a spec defect underneath the naming:

004 §"Delegated Bridge Signing" (:113-122) defines a delegate certificate with `KeyUsage: digitalSignature only`, and in the next line says it "enables local bridge cert issuance without public root online", with relying parties required to accept it as an intermediate between the public root and the bridge cert.

Those cannot both hold. Issuing certificates requires keyCertSign; a certificate carrying digitalSignature only cannot be a valid issuer, and any RFC 5280-conformant path validator will reject a chain through it. Either the delegate is meant to issue — in which case it needs keyCertSign and IsCA:true, making it an Issuing CA and confirming notme's point about the name — or it is not meant to issue, in which case "enables local bridge cert issuance" is wrong and the three-tier chain in that section does not work as described.

This is the same CA-versus-leaf confusion this bead exists to fix, appearing inside the ADR that defines the vocabulary. Which is some evidence the confusion originated there rather than drifting in later.

Mitigating context: 004 already carries an implementation note (:7-9) conceding the deployed certificates do not implement its ASN.1 structure, so this may never have shipped. But 004 is what a reader is pointed at, so a reader can still build the wrong verifier from it. Fixing the KeyUsage/issuance contradiction should happen in the same pass as the rename, not after it.
comments.author: rsry-mcp

acceptance_criteria: Each of the four artifacts has a distinct name stating its X.509 shape; docs/design/004-bridge-certs.md either describes a shipped artifact or is marked superseded; no document calls an end-entity certificate a CA or vice versa; and the decision is recorded somewhere notme can cite so 0.2 can be closed.

title: Add tests for pkg/git/sign.go and pkg/git/verify.go
description:
## What

pkg/git has only one test file (identity_test.go). The CMS/PKCS#7 signing logic in sign.go and verification logic in verify.go have zero direct unit tests.

## Why

Critical signing paths are untested:
- `signWithBridgeCert` (sign.go:66) — 3-cert chain signing (Level 1+)
- `signWithEphemeralCert` (sign.go ~line 30) — Level 0 backward-compat path

The integration test (test_integration.sh) exercises end-to-end git signing but does not give per-function coverage or regression protection for refactors. Surgical review of signet-8915ba (ADR-007 Level 1+) flagged this in `_agent_log/surgical-reviewer_2026-03-16_agent_log.md` as a [High] issue; identity_test.go was added later but sign/verify still lack unit tests.

## Code citations

- `pkg/git/sign.go:66` — `signWithBridgeCert` untested

- `pkg/git/verify.go` — entire file untested

`_agent_log/surgical-reviewer_2026-03-16_agent_log.md` issue #6

comments.text:
Phase 1 (pure-function unit tests) shipped in `test/pkg-git-coverage` (commit 9c6990f, PR opened).

**Covered (10 tests):**
- `certHexFingerprint` — 3 tests: nil cert → all-zero, empty `Raw` → all-zero, deterministic SHA-1 hex of `cert.Raw` (40 chars, idempotent)
- `emitStatus` — 3 tests: `statusFd<=0` is a no-op (covers fd=0 and fd=-1), `statusFd>0` writes the line to the fd (verified via `os.Pipe`)
- `getStatusWriter` — 4 tests: fd=0 → `os.Stderr` (the documented "prevent stdout pollution" default), fd=1 → `os.Stdout`, fd=2 → `os.Stderr` (gpgsm/gitsign fd convention), custom fd → `*os.File` wrapping that fd with `cleanup()` that actually closes the file (verified via `os.Pipe` + post-cleanup write fails)

All pass under `-race` and `go vet`.

**Not yet covered (Phase 2, recommended as a follow-up bead):**
The end-to-end `SignCommit → VerifySignature` roundtrip — `signLevel0` (2-cert chain) and `signWithBridgeCert` (3-cert chain). This needs:
- A test `Identity` constructed with an in-memory master key (+ optional bridge cert + bridge key)
- `stdin` redirection of commit bytes into `SignCommit`, `stdout` capture of the PEM-encoded `SIGNED MESSAGE` block
- The output piped back into `VerifySignature` against the same master key

The Docker-resident `scripts/testing/test_integration.sh` already exercises the full git-commit signing path end-to-end, so the existence of CMS-roundtrip coverage is not zero — but a focused Go-level test would lock in the API contract (cert chain depth, status fd output format, error paths) more cheaply than the Docker test. Worth filing as P2 follow-up.

This bead can stay open until the roundtrip phase ships, or close on PR merge with a new bead spawned for Phase 2 — your call.

title: Register IANA PEN — replace OID placeholder 1.3.6.1.4.1.99999
description:
## What

The signet OID arc `1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.1.*` is a placeholder. Before public release, an IANA Private Enterprise Number must be registered and all OID constants updated.

## Why

Using 99999 risks collision with any other ad-hoc user of the same arc, and certificates issued today will need to be re-issued (or the OID values aliased) once a real PEN is allocated.

## Code citations

- `pkg/sigid/identity.go:38` — `OIDSubject = []int{1, 3, 6, 1, 4, 1, 99999, 1, 1}`
- `pkg/sigid/identity.go:41` — `OIDIssuanceTime`
- `pkg/sigid/identity.go:49` — `OIDAgentName`
- `pkg/sigid/identity.go:55` — `OIDScope`
- `pkg/attest/x509/bridge.go` — `OIDSignetCapabilities` at `1.3.6.1.4.1.99999.1.3`
- `rig/web/src/auth/signet-edge.ts` — same arc on TS edge minting path
- `cmd/signet/verify.go` — `extractExtValue` reads all four OIDs

1. Apply for IANA PEN (https://pen.iana.org/pen/PenApplication.page)
2. Update OID constants in `pkg/sigid/identity.go` and `pkg/attest/x509/bridge.go`

title: basic.Provider stubs: extractEnvironment / extractBoundary return empty

- `pkg/sigid/providers/basic/provider.go:122-129` — `extractBoundary` returns empty Boundary with `// TODO: Extract from field 22`

The cell provider (`pkg/sigid/providers/cell/`) does deserialize these fields; the basic provider should do the same for non-cell tokens or be explicitly documented as field-20-or-bust.

## Why

The 4-entity model documented in ADR-010 and sigid-requirements.md treats Environment and Boundary as first-class Pillar 4 sub-dimensions. Today only cell-tokens carry them.

## Source

`docs/design/sigid-requirements.md` §2.2 and §2.3

comments.text:
Doc-clarification path landed in `chore/signet-doc-triage-followups` (commit 858efdb).

**Why doc-clarification, not implementation:** The typed `*signet.Token` struct (pkg/signet/token.go) currently exposes CBOR fields 1-19 only. Field 20 (Provenance), 21 (Environment), 22 (Boundary) are not on the typed struct. The cell provider reads them via raw CBOR map decode (`cell.Provider.ExtractContextFromCBOR` → `cbor.Unmarshal(payload, &map[int]interface{}{})`). So basic.Provider's `extractEnvironment`/`extractBoundary` cannot read fields 20-22 from the typed shape — that is an architectural reality, not forgotten TODO work.

**What this commit does:**
- Replaces bare `TODO: extract from field N` comments with full method docs explaining the typed-Token-stops-at-19 reality
- Cross-references `cell.Provider.extractEnvironmentFromMap` / `extractBoundaryFromMap` as the reference pattern
- Spells out the two viable wiring paths: (a) add typed accessors to `signet.Token`, or (b) add an `ExtractContextFromCBOR` variant to `basic.Provider`
- Same treatment for the field-20 TODO in `extractProvenance`

No behavior change. `go build ./...` clean, `go test ./pkg/sigid/...` all green.

**Follow-up question for product:** If basic.Provider needs to read fields 20-22 in practice, that is real feature work (probably P2, not the P3 scope of this bead). Worth filing as a separate "wire Token typed accessors for sigid fields 20-22" bead if/when a consumer surfaces.

Closing as resolved at the doc-clarity level — the stubs are no longer misleading.

title: BoundaryValidator interface defined but never used (region validation missing)
description:
## What

The `BoundaryValidator` interface is defined at `pkg/sigid/provider.go:33-34` but no implementation uses it. The cell provider inlines VPC CIDR + domain validation directly instead of going through the interface, and region validation is unimplemented entirely.

## Code citations

- `pkg/sigid/provider.go:33` — `type BoundaryValidator interface { ... }` (defined, never imported anywhere)
- `pkg/sigid/providers/cell/provider.go` — inline VPC/domain validation, no Region check

## Action

- Either remove the unused interface (YAGNI) and let cell provider keep inline validation
- Or implement the interface (VPCValidator, RegionValidator, DomainValidator) and have cell provider compose them

## Why

Unused interfaces drift over time. ADR-010 §6 mentions Region validation requires cloud-provider metadata; documenting "Region validation requires cloud metadata, not implemented" is honest, while the empty interface gives a false impression of pluggability.

## Source

`docs/design/sigid-requirements.md` §2.3

title: Keystore UX: rename --insecure → --keystore-backend, expose ephemeral mode for testing/CI
description:
## What

`signet-git init` writes to the OS keyring (Keychain on macOS, Secret Service on Linux) by default and has no clean way to materialize an ephemeral/test keystore without `--insecure`. The flag is misnamed for the actual use case.

## Concrete UX gap

```
$ signet-git init --home $TMPDIR/signet-test
initialization failed: master key already exists in keyring (use --force to overwrite)
```

- `--home` is silently ignored — keyring is global per-user, no namespacing
- The only "isolated" path is `--insecure`, which clobbers home `master.key` with no auth, BUT in a tmpdir+chmod-600 file it is **not** less secure than a shared system keyring — it is just *different*
- `--insecure` framing actively discourages the path that should be the canonical test/CI mode
- No `--keystore=ephemeral` or `--keystore=memory` mode for true throwaway keys

## Why this matters

1. **Testability**: cannot dogfood `signet-git` sign→verify roundtrip in CI without either (a) clobbering the developer's real master key with `--force`, or (b) following the `--insecure` path which the help text actively warns against.
2. **Integration tests**: `scripts/testing/test_integration.sh` runs in Docker (no keyring), so it already takes the `--insecure` path implicitly. The naming makes the test path look like a hack.
3. **CI on macOS/Linux runners**: keyring access in headless runners is flaky (Linux requires dbus + gnome-keyring; macOS Keychain needs unlock). The current default-to-keyring + opt-out-via-`--insecure` design forces every CI workflow to know about the workaround.

## Proposed design (sketch — needs ADR-level decision)

**Option A: Rename + reframe**
```
signet-git init                                # auto-detect: keyring if available, else file
signet-git init --keystore=keyring             # explicit keyring
signet-git init --keystore=file --home <path>  # explicit file (replaces --insecure)
signet-git init --keystore=ephemeral           # tmpfs, never persisted
```
Deprecate `--insecure` (keep as hidden alias for one release).

**Option B: Namespaced keyring**
Allow `--service-name=signet-test-XXXX` to namespace within the keyring. Solves test isolation without leaving the secure backend. More invasive — needs keyring entry-cleanup story.

**Option C: Hybrid**
- `--home` always wins (when set, force file-based regardless of keyring availability)
- Rename `--insecure` → `--file-keystore` or just remove the flag in favor of `--home`-implies-file

## Acceptance criteria

- A new contributor can run a sign→verify roundtrip against signet-git from a fresh clone without touching their real keyring
- `scripts/testing/test_integration.sh` no longer needs to pass `--insecure` (the flag is gone or the path is the documented default for test contexts)
- The help text for the chosen flag does not describe the test path as "insecure"

## Discovered by

Dogfooding PR #126 (pkg/git unit tests). User flag: "we need to actually use the code and not trust tests only" — the immediate friction was that there's no clean way to run signet-git against an ephemeral keystore.

## Out of scope

- Hardware-backed keystores (Touch ID signer, PKCS#11) — those are different backends, tracked separately
- The keyring service-name collision question (signet vs notme on the same machine) — separate concern

## Files likely touched

- `cmd/signet-git/init.go` (or wherever the init subcommand lives)
- `pkg/cli/keystore/secure.go`
- `pkg/cli/keystore/insecure.go` (if it exists; if not, the file-based loader)
- Help text + README pointers
- Possibly an ADR in `docs/design/` if the change is breaking

comments.text:
**Additional finding from dogfooding PR #126:**

Even with `signet-git init --home <isolated> --insecure` succeeding (writes `master.key` to the isolated home), subsequent `signet-git export-key-id --home <isolated>` returns the user's **real** keyring KID, not the isolated home's KID.

Root cause: `pkg/cli/keystore` load-priority is hardcoded as **keyring first, file fallback**:

```go
// pkg/git/verify.go:withMasterKeyForVerify (mirrors sign path)
masterKey, err := keystore.LoadMasterKeySecure()        // always tries keyring first
if err != nil {
    // SECURITY: Validate home path before using it for file-based key loading
    masterKey, err = keystore.LoadMasterKeyInsecure(cfg.Home)
}
```

So `--home` is functionally a fallback path — it only takes effect when the keyring is **unavailable** (Docker, headless CI). On a developer's local machine where signet has ever been initialized into the keyring, every subsequent `signet-git` call against any `--home` will load the keyring's master key, not the home's `master.key`.

**Consequences:**

1. The current dogfood workaround (init isolated home with `--insecure`, then sign/verify against it) does **not** actually use the isolated key — it uses the user's real master key. The signing/verify code paths *are* exercised end-to-end (PR #126 dogfooded successfully and produced a valid CMS signature), but the test does not actually isolate from the user's real identity.

2. `scripts/testing/test_integration.sh` runs in Docker (no keyring), so it accidentally takes the file path correctly. But any developer running the integration test locally would silently sign against their real keyring key.

3. The CLI surface implies `--home` selects the keystore; the implementation does not.

**Add to the design:** the `--keystore=file|keyring|ephemeral` option needs to be an **override**, not a hint. When `--keystore=file` is passed (or `--home` is explicitly set in a future cleaner design), the keyring must be skipped entirely — both for read AND write paths. Otherwise the "isolated test" abstraction is a lie.

Files touched would expand to include `pkg/cli/keystore/secure.go` (the load function) and every call site of `LoadMasterKeySecure()` that should respect a keystore-backend override.
comments.author: rsry-mcp

comments.text:
**Update 2026-05-19 — user suggests XDG-based design (simpler than the original `--keystore=` flag proposal)**

Standard Unix convention beats a new flag. The fix:

```
XDG_CONFIG_HOME=$(mktemp -d) signet-git init   # writes there, no keyring touch
XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=$(mktemp -d) signet-git init   # ephemeral (tmpfs on Linux)
```

Every CI runner and integration-test harness already understands XDG; tools like `gh`, `gpg`, `gnupg-modern`, `pass` all respect it. No new flag, no new mental model.

## But XDG alone isn't the whole fix

The dogfooding finding (additional comment on this bead) showed that even with `--home /tmp/...` set, `LoadMasterKeySecure()` hits the OS keyring **first** regardless of the home path. XDG_CONFIG_HOME would have the same problem: it'd direct *writes* to the XDG path but *reads* would still try the keyring first.

The complete fix needs two parts:

1. **Path routing (XDG)** — when `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is set, use `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/signet/` as the keystore root for both writes (init) and reads (load).
2. **Load-priority routing** — when an XDG path is set OR an explicit file path exists, file beats keyring (or keyring is skipped entirely). Otherwise current keyring-first behavior is preserved.

Concretely, `pkg/cli/keystore/secure.go:LoadMasterKeySecure` and every caller need to either:
- (a) accept a `KeystoreSource` enum (`file | keyring | auto`), defaulting to auto with XDG-implies-file, or
- (b) check for `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/signet/master.key` and short-circuit before the keyring lookup.

(b) is the minimum-viable change.

## Acceptance criteria (updated)

- `XDG_CONFIG_HOME=$(mktemp -d) signet-git init` writes `master.key` to that path and **does not** touch the OS keyring
- `XDG_CONFIG_HOME=$(mktemp -d) signet-git export-key-id` returns the KID for the XDG-home key, **not** the user's real keyring key
- `scripts/testing/test_integration.sh` can drop the `--insecure` flag entirely (or the flag is deprecated → no-op)
- Help text no longer describes the test path as "insecure"
- Backwards compat: when XDG vars are unset, current keyring-first behavior is preserved bit-for-bit

## What this drops from the original proposal

- The `--keystore=file|keyring|ephemeral` flag. XDG covers `file` and `ephemeral` (via `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`); keyring is the unset-default.
- Custom service-name namespacing inside the keyring (the "Option B" in the original). Not needed if XDG handles isolation.

## What stays

- `--insecure` flag rename/deprecation. Eventually a no-op once XDG handles the test path.
- Audit of `LoadMasterKeySecure()` call sites — every read path needs the same load-priority logic.

title: gha-identity.yml is a diverged local copy of notme's — reconcile or consume the original
description:
signet-resign.yml:34 calls `uses: ./.github/workflows/gha-identity.yml` — a LOCAL copy, not agentic-research/notme's. The two have already diverged: notme's exposes `notme_token` and `expires_in` outputs that signet's does not, and their audience descriptions differ. signet's copy even self-references `agentic-research/signet/...` in its own usage example.

Both implement the same exchange — one GHA OIDC token becomes an octo-sts-scoped GitHub App token plus a notme bridge cert — and both ultimately call the same live service at auth.notme.bot. signet's exists to eliminate SIGNET_MASTER_KEY; notme's to eliminate stored PATs. Same idea, two hand-maintained implementations, already drifting.

WHY THIS IS WORTH TRACKING RATHER THAN SHRUGGING AT. It is another instance of the pattern catalogued in vigil's release-contract design (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-27-release-contract-design.md sections 1.2 and 8.1): one good idea implemented independently in several repos, with no shared source, drifting quietly. The others found so far are post-publish verification (LLO, mache), tag-manifest version gating (LLO, mache, canonical-hours, notme), and regen-diff drift gating (LLO, cloister, rosary). This is the identity-primitive instance, and it is the most security-sensitive of them, since divergence in an auth exchange is not a cosmetic difference.

Note the direction of dependency: notme is the TS live auth service implementing the model; signet is the Go client. So signet consuming notme's reusable workflow (`uses: agentic-research/notme/.github/workflows/gha-identity.yml@<sha>`) is the natural shape, not the reverse. notme is private, so verify a private repo's reusable workflow is callable from signet before committing to that direction — if it is not, the fallback is a documented sync with a drift check, in the idiom cloister's generated-drift.yml and rosary's taskfile-contract already establish.

Decide: consume notme's directly, or keep a local copy with an explicit drift gate and a comment saying why. What should not persist is an undeclared copy that silently diverges.

Surfaced 2026-07-28 by adversarial review of the vigil release-contract spec, which had incorrectly stated that signet consumes notme's primitive. Verified directly at signet-resign.yml:34.

comments.text: Goal Zero release review (signet-cf2adc) findings, verified 2026-08-05: (1) The bead's premise that notme is private is WRONG — gh repo view confirms agentic-research/notme is public, so consuming notme's reusable workflow directly is viable. (2) But the drift is worse than described: notme's .github/workflows/gha-identity.yml:57-66 declares outputs notme_token and expires_in while notme/action/action.yml emits notme_url/notme_cert/notme_signing_cert/notme_identity/expires_at — BOTH of notme's advertised outputs resolve to empty strings. The action's shape changed at notme f171e8d; notme's workflow still pins the action at e57c9ad (2026-05-10). (3) Signet holds the CORRECTED fork (authority_url input, real output set, action pinned at 1ccd3b0), and rig already consumes signet's version (rig/.github/workflows/deploy.yml:27). Resolution direction: fix flows signet → notme (upstream signet's corrections), then consumers can converge on notme's canonical copy. (4) The drift has a live casualty: signet-resign.yml reads bridge_cert/bridge_key which no version emits any more — filed as signet-e6cbea. Classification for signet-c0a34f: ADVISORY for the artifact release train (nothing in release.yml consumes gha-identity.yml), BLOCKING for the resign flow.
comments.author: rsry-mcp

comments.text:
THIS BEAD'S PREMISE HAS CHANGED — and the direction of the divergence was the opposite of what it assumed. From notme's Goal Zero cross-repo audit (notme-c0a4aa).

WHAT THE AUDIT FOUND: signet's local copy was the CORRECT interface and notme's original was broken. notme's gha-identity.yml declared outputs `notme_token` and `expires_in`, and notme's action/ emits NEITHER — it outputs a cert pair plus `expires_at` (action/src/index.ts, action.yml). Both resolved to the empty string for every caller. So this bead's "consume the original" option would have been a REGRESSION: signet would have adopted a workflow whose identity-bearing outputs are always empty.

It survived unnoticed because notme's only caller of that workflow is test-identity.yml, which is workflow_dispatch-only, asserts nothing, and last ran green weeks before the action's output shape changed.

FIXED ON NOTME'S SIDE (commit dc24f69 on notme's goalzero branch, PR #70). notme's workflow now declares notme_cert, notme_signing_cert, notme_identity and expires_at, matching what the action actually emits, and a gate (worker/src/__tests__/gha-identity-outputs.test.ts) checks all four directions: workflow→job, job→action.yml, src→action.yml, and action.yml→src. That last direction found a second live instance — action.yml declared a `github_token` output that src never sets.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THIS BEAD: "consume the original" becomes viable once notme's fix reaches main, where before it was the wrong choice. Both options in the AC are now genuinely open rather than one being a trap. If you keep the local copy, the drift check the AC already contemplates is the right shape — and note that notme's copy is the one that drifted, so the check protects both directions.

RELATED, and worth knowing before you decide: notme's gha-identity.yml pins its OWN action by SHA, and that pin had rotted through three merged PRs (notme-28959a). notme now has scripts/check-self-pins.ts comparing the pinned action/ tree against the default branch, wired into `task pin:check`. If signet consumes notme's workflow by SHA, the same staleness question applies to signet's pin of it — signet currently pins notme/action at 1ccd3b0, which predates a security rebuild of action/dist that fixed three undici advisories (GHSA-8xcm-r25x-g524, GHSA-m8rv-5g2x-5cg5, GHSA-v3r7-h72x-cjcm). That pin needs to advance regardless of how this bead resolves.

acceptance_criteria: Either signet-resign.yml references notme's reusable workflow by owner/repo at a pinned SHA and the local copy is deleted, or the local copy remains with a CI drift check that fails when it diverges from notme's and a comment stating why a copy is kept. In both cases a real run of signet-resign.yml succeeds with the chosen arrangement.

title: signet auth login: support browser-initiated keypair + bridge cert flow
description:
signet auth login works great as a CLI tool (localhost callback, PKCE, auto-configure Claude Code). But the same flow needs to work from a browser context too — for users who hit /sign-in on rosary.bot.

**Current CLI flow (working):**
1. Generate ECDSA P-256 keypair locally
2. Start localhost:random/callback server
3. Open browser → rosary.bot/oauth/authorize → Clerk
4. Receive code at callback, exchange for token
5. POST pubkey to /api/cert, get bridge cert
6. Save cert+key to ~/.signet/mcp/rosary/

**Needed browser flow:**
1. Browser generates keypair via WebCrypto (P-256 or Ed25519)
2. User authenticates via Clerk (already on /sign-in)
3. Browser POSTs pubkey to /api/cert/bootstrap (authenticated via Clerk session)
4. Receives signed bridge cert
5. User downloads cert+key bundle (or we offer `signet auth import` to pull from server)

**Key question:** How does the browser-generated private key get to the user's machine for CLI use? Options:
- Download as .pem file (simple, user copies to ~/.signet/mcp/)
- `signet auth import --from-browser` fetches cert from a short-lived KV slot
- QR code / deep link that signet CLI catches

This connects to sigid: once user has bridge cert, sigid extracts identity claims from it. The cert is the root of trust — everything else is derived.

Relates: rig /sign-in bead, signet-1c457e (runtime split)

comments.text: Overlap check (2026-04-12): References auth_login.go (shared with signet-34def0 tracking bead only). No conflicts — 34def0 is passive tracking. This bead adds browser flow, independent of authority refactor. Can proceed when ready.

title: Design: cert-as-root-of-trust — what claims go in X.509 vs sigid CBOR fields
description:
Core architectural question: the bridge cert is the "door key" — proof you're authenticated. Everything else should be derivable. But WHERE do the derived claims live?

**Option A: Claims in X.509 extensions**
- Embed sigid context (provenance, boundary, environment) as X.509 v3 extensions in the bridge cert
- Pro: CF WAF can evaluate extensions at edge, no second lookup
- Con: cert is immutable once issued, can't update claims without reissuing
- Con: X.509 extension OIDs need registration, tooling is painful

**Option B: Claims alongside cert (sigid's current approach)**
- Bridge cert identifies the user (CN=user-{id}, pubkey binding)
- sigid fields (CBOR 20-23) travel in the PoP token, not the cert
- Pro: claims can vary per-request (different boundary for different endpoints)
- Pro: cert stays simple, sigid is the flexible layer
- Con: need both cert AND token for full context

**Option C: Hybrid — minimal claims in cert, rich claims in sigid**
- Cert carries: user ID, issuer, tier (stable claims)
- sigid carries: boundary, environment, delegation chain (dynamic claims)
- ley-line uses cert identity to look up arena permissions
- rosary uses sigid context for dispatch authorization

The connection to ley-line: ley-line manifests are already signed with Ed25519. If the user's bridge cert identity matches ley-line arena permissions, that's the authorization chain: signet cert → sigid context → ley-line access.

Depends on: sigid environment/boundary implementation (fields 21-22, currently stubbed)

comments.text: Decided on Option C (hybrid) during session. Cert carries stable identity (owner, issuer, issuance time via OID 99999.1.{1,2}). sigid carries dynamic context (boundary, environment, delegation) via CBOR fields 20-23. Implemented in PRs #97-#101. This bead is now a documentation task — write the formal ADR.
comments.author: rsry-mcp

comments.text: Staleness check (2026-04-12): pkg/signet/token.go now has MaxTokenLifetime = 10min validation. Any design that involves long-lived tokens (cert-embedded claims) must work within this constraint or explicitly bypass it. Also: binding message format changed (purpose field now length-prefixed) — existing binding signatures won't verify.

title: CABundle wire-format divergence: pick canonical-bytes encoding (CBOR-only or JSON-only) and deprecate the other
description:
## Carved off from signet-683223 (closed in PR #128)

The discoverability part of signet-683223 shipped in `docs/design/cross-language-schema.md`. The remaining functional bug is this bead.

## What

`CABundle` is signed in two cryptographically non-interoperable ways across the signet ecosystem:

- **Go (`pkg/revocation/checker.go:168-188`):** canonical CBOR per RFC 8949 §4.2, integer-keyed map
- **TypeScript clients (per the original signet-683223 body):** JSON with alphabetical key sort

These produce different byte sequences over identical logical content, so a `CABundle` signed in one language fails verification silently in the other. Schema-parity in `notme/schema/identity.capnp` does not resolve this — schema parity ≠ wire-format parity.

## Acceptance criteria

- Pick one canonical wire format; update `docs/design/cross-language-schema.md` "Open contract gap (deferred)" callout
- Deprecate or remove the losing format with a stated cutover window
- Add a cross-language test vector (preferably `notme/schema/test-vectors/cabundle/`) proving identical bytes in Go + TypeScript
- Both verifiers reject the deprecated format (or accept it during cutover with a log entry)

## Why this is hard

- JSON+alphabetical-sort is fragile (nested-object key ordering, floats, whitespace); CBOR §4.2 is more battle-tested
- Need to inventory which side has production consumers before deciding which to deprecate
- Cutover affects every existing signed bundle in the losing format

## Discovered by

Body of signet-683223 (P0, closed 2026-05-19). Discoverability part shipped in PR #128 (commit 5f80794); this remaining functional gap was explicitly deferred per "nothing functional ideally" direction.

comments.text:
**Related: signet-2f6b68** (capnp-ify MasterKeyDescriptor)

Per user observation 2026-05-19: both beads are the same architectural hole — **the capnp schema carries types but not canonical bytes**. Together:

- **This bead (bdaf24):** type IS in schema, signed two ways. Pick one canonical encoding.
- **Sibling (2f6b68):** type is NOT in schema, lives signet-side only. Promote it in.

**Combined fix shape:** add a canonical-bytes annotation to `identity.capnp` (e.g. `$canonicalEncoding("cbor-rfc8949-deterministic")`) as part of resolving bdaf24. Then any subsequent promotion (2f6b68 and others) inherits the wire-format contract by virtue of being in the schema. This makes the schema-bridge the single source of truth for *both* shape and bytes, which is the whole point of having a schema.

title: signet-resign.yml has not completed a successful run since May — the post-merge re-signing path is unverified
description:
Found 2026-08-07 while advancing the notme action pin (notme-28959a, PR #173). The pin advance is correct by inspection of the bundle, but NOT by observation, because nothing exercises the path.

## Run history

    30957051279  pull_request_review  agent/signet-579491-ci-signing     action_required  2026-08-04
    30941531289  pull_request_review  signet-9b0ecd-sign-releases        action_required  2026-08-04
    26066994449  pull_request_review  chore/substrate-idl-signet         failure          2026-05-18
    26066992610  ... failure / cancelled x6                                               2026-05-18

Last non-failing outcome predates 2026-05-18. The two most recent runs ended `action_required` (gated, never executed). No green run exists in the visible history.

## Why it matters beyond the workflow itself

signet-resign.yml is the ONLY caller of gha-identity.yml, which is `on: workflow_call` and therefore has no trigger of its own. So the entire chain — octo-sts token exchange, the pinned notme action, the bridge-cert exchange — is dead code in practice:

- The undici 6.25.0 exposure (notme-28959a) named signet as a consumer executing the bundle with an OIDC identity in scope. In signet that never actually happened in a passing run.
- The freshly advanced pin (f35a46a8) has no run that proves it works.
- `signet authority setup-resign` is a DOCUMENTED CLI command whose output configures this workflow. We ship a command that configures a path we have never seen succeed.

This is the same family as signet-71d9d8 (oidc-signing.yml is not a production canary): a green-looking piece of supply-chain machinery that is not actually sampling what it claims to sample. Here it is worse — it is not green, and nobody noticed for ~3 months, because `pull_request_review` fires rarely and its failures are not surfaced anywhere.

## What to determine

1. Why the 2026-05-18 runs failed (logs are past retention for at least one run id — check what remains).
2. Why the 2026-08-04 runs were `action_required` — likely the approval gate for a workflow requiring secrets from a branch, but confirm rather than assume.
3. Whether post-merge re-signing is still wanted at all. If yes, it needs a trigger that actually fires and a failure that is visible. If no, delete the workflow AND the `signet authority setup-resign` command together — shipping a configurator for a deleted path is worse than either alone.

Do not close by making the workflow green once by hand. The defect is that its health was unobservable for three months; a single manual green run reproduces exactly that condition.
